name: Barnabas
bio: Joses, a Levite from Cyprus surnamed Barnabas ("son of consolation") by the apostles, sold his land and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet for distribution to those in need (Acts 4:36-37). His far larger role in the early church and alongside Paul is told in detail in the chapters ahead. When Saul, newly converted, tried to join the Jerusalem disciples, they were afraid of him until Barnabas took him to the apostles and vouched for his encounter with the Lord and his bold preaching in Damascus (Acts 9:26-27). Sent by the Jerusalem church to Antioch, where many Gentiles had begun believing, Barnabas rejoiced at their faith and encouraged them to remain devoted to the Lord; he then went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him back to Antioch, where the two taught together for a year, and the believers there were first called Christians. When the prophet Agabus foretold a coming famine, Barnabas and Saul were entrusted with carrying relief from the Antioch believers to those in Judea (Acts 11:19-30). At Antioch, the Holy Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for missionary work, and after fasting and prayer the church sent them off with the laying on of hands. They sailed to Cyprus with John Mark as their minister, preaching in the synagogues, and at Paphos confronted the sorcerer Bar-jesus, who was trying to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith; Sergius Paulus believed after the sorcerer was struck blind. In Antioch of Pisidia, Barnabas and Paul preached boldly to a receptive crowd, but when the Jews responded with envy and contradiction, the two declared that they would turn to the Gentiles instead, as the Lord had commanded; many believed, though persecution eventually drove them out to Iconium (Acts 13:1-52). At Lystra, after Paul healed a man crippled from birth, the crowds hailed Barnabas and Paul as gods, calling Barnabas "Jupiter" and Paul "Mercurius," and moved to offer sacrifice; the two tore their clothes in protest and barely restrained them, insisting they were mere men preaching the living God. Barnabas and Paul then endured Paul's stoning at Lystra, continued preaching through Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch appointing elders, and returned to report to the church at Antioch in Syria how God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles (Acts 14:1-28). When believers from Judea insisted that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved, Barnabas and Paul took the dispute to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, where the two reported the miracles God had worked among the Gentiles through them; the council sided with Peter and James, requiring only a few basic restrictions, and sent Barnabas and Paul back to Antioch with Judas Barsabas and Silas carrying the decision in writing (Acts 15:1-35). Some time later, Barnabas wanted to take John Mark along on a return visit to the churches, but Paul refused, since Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia; the disagreement grew so sharp that the two separated, and Barnabas sailed for Cyprus with Mark while Paul took Silas instead (Acts 15:36-41).
